acoes.txt: Define the error metric and the target value from the problem the application solves; the metric guides future actions.
Remember the Bayes error: the minimum achievable error even with infinite data (incomplete features, stochasticity, finite data).

Asymmetric costs and rare events: use total cost, precision/recall (F = 2pr/(p+r)) and/or coverage instead of accuracy alone; an 'always absent' classifier has 99.9999% accuracy on a 1-in-1-million event.
Define the metric BEFORE optimizing; without clear goals you cannot tell whether a change makes progress.
Build an end-to-end system as early as possible, with the estimated metrics.
If a few linear weights can solve it, start with a simple statistical model (logistic regression); 'AI-complete' problems (objects, speech, translation) start with an appropriate deep learning model.
Fixed-size vectors: fully connected feedforward; input with topology (image): CNN; sequence: LSTM or GRU. Piecewise linear units (ReLU and generalizations).

Optimizer: SGD with momentum and decaying learning rate (linear down to a minimum, exponential, or divide by 2-10 when validation plateaus) or Adam. Batch normalization can be left out of the 1st baseline but comes in soon if optimization is problematic.
Mild regularization from the start, unless training has tens of millions of examples; early stopping almost universal; dropout is a good regularizer.

If the task resembles one already studied, copy the known model/algorithm (even a trained model). Unsupervised learning in the 1st baseline only if known to be important in the domain (e.g. word embeddings in NLP).

subajuste.titulo: 3a. Poor training performance: do not collect more data yet

acoes.txt: The algorithm is not using the data it already has: there is no reason to collect more data.
Rule out software defects: try fitting a tiny dataset (one example); compare backprop derivatives with finite differences; look at histograms of activations and gradients.
If there is no regularization and optimization works, increase capacity (more layers or more hidden units).
Tune the learning rate (the most important hyperparameter): too high increases the error, too low can get stuck at high error.
Check the optimization: update/parameter ratio around 1% (not 50%, nor 0.001%); saturated or always-off units.
Consider batch normalization, momentum or Adam if optimization is the bottleneck.

qualidade.titulo: 3b. Do large, well-tuned models still fail?
qualidade.pergunta: Even with a larger model and tuned optimization, does the training error remain high?

acoes.txt: The data may be noisy or may not contain the right inputs: start over by collecting cleaner data or a richer set of features.
Visualize the worst errors (the most confident ones): they reveal preprocessing or labeling problems (Street View example: a tight crop omitted digits).
Go back to the node 'is the training error acceptable?' with the new model/optimization.

pronto.titulo: Nothing more to do (for this target)

acoes.txt: If the test error is also acceptable, there is nothing more to do.

gap.titulo: 4a. Large gap between training and test (overfitting)

acoes.txt: First: confirm that the difference is real - test error can come from saving/reloading the model or from preprocessing the test set differently from training.
Collecting more data is one of the most effective solutions if cost and feasibility allow it (internet companies: almost always).
Alternative to collecting data: shrink the model or improve regularization (weight decay, dropout); the best performance usually comes from a large, well-regularized model; early stopping.
If the gap persists after tuning regularization, collecting more data is advisable.

How much to collect: plot error vs training set size (like Fig. 5.4) and extrapolate; experiment on a logarithmic scale (double the number of examples between experiments); adding a small fraction does not noticeably change the error.
Without additional data and with regularization exhausted, improving the algorithm is a research question, not applied advice.

Manual: match the effective capacity to the complexity of the task (representational capacity, the algorithm's ability to minimize the cost, and degree of regularization). Table 11.1 summarizes what increases capacity.

Automatic: grid search for up to 3 hyperparameters (values on a log scale; cost O(n^m)); random search (log-uniform distribution, no discretization) is more efficient; Bayesian optimization is not unequivocally recommended.
Visualize the model in action (detections, samples) and the worst errors.
Reason with training and test error: low training + high test = overfitting or a test measurement error; both high = faulty software OR underfitting (needs more tests).

Fit a tiny dataset (one example); compare backprop with numerical derivatives (centered difference; random projections u and v; complex step); monitor histograms; test the algorithm's guarantees with tolerance.
